title: How I Finally Apologized to My Oldest Friend
script: Narrator: [honestly] Six months ago, I said something careless to my friend Andi during a stressful week, and I watched our friendship quietly change afterward.
Narrator: [thoughtful] I had criticized his business decision in front of other friends, without thinking about how embarrassing that must have felt for him.
Narrator: [reflective] He didn't yell or argue with me that night. He simply grew quieter, and something between us shifted almost immediately.
Narrator: [honestly] Afterward, he replied to my messages more slowly, and eventually, he mostly stopped replying at all.
Narrator: [thoughtful] I told myself he was probably just busy, because admitting I had hurt him felt uncomfortable and difficult to face directly.
Narrator: [gently] Meanwhile, I kept replaying that evening in my head, noticing more clearly each time how unnecessary my comment really was.
Narrator: [honestly] Pride kept stopping me from apologizing properly, because part of me still believed my original point had actually been correct.
Narrator: [reflective] But being right, I slowly realized, meant nothing if it cost me twenty years of genuine friendship in the process.
Narrator: [determined] So last week, I finally invited him for coffee, and I told him directly that I regretted embarrassing him that night.
Narrator: [nervous] My hands were actually shaking a little while I spoke, because I genuinely didn't know how he would respond to me.
Narrator: [relieved] He was quiet for a moment, and then he admitted he had been waiting for me to say exactly that, for months.
Narrator: [warmly] We talked for almost two hours after that, about the argument, about his business, about everything we had avoided discussing.
Narrator: [peacefully] I learned that apologies rarely become easier by waiting longer. They usually just become heavier, and harder to finally say out loud.
Narrator: [with a small smile] Andi and I still disagree sometimes, honestly, but now we actually talk about it, instead of quietly disappearing from each other's lives.

quiz.question: What did the narrator do that damaged his friendship with Andi?
options: He borrowed money and didn't repay it
He criticized Andi's business decision in front of other friends
He forgot Andi's birthday
He moved away without telling him
quiz.explanation: He had criticized Andi's business decision in front of other friends, embarrassing him.

quiz.question: How did Andi react that night?
options: He yelled and argued
He grew quiet, and things shifted between them
He laughed it off
He immediately ended the friendship
quiz.explanation: Andi didn't argue; he simply grew quieter, and something shifted between them that night.

quiz.question: What kept the narrator from apologizing sooner?
options: He didn't know Andi's phone number
Pride, because he still believed his original point was correct
He forgot about the incident
Andi asked him not to apologize
quiz.explanation: Pride kept stopping him, since part of him still believed his original point had been correct.

quiz.question: How did Andi respond when the narrator finally apologized?
options: He said he had been waiting to hear that for months
He refused to accept the apology
He said it didn't matter to him
He ended the friendship anyway
quiz.explanation: Andi admitted he had been waiting for the narrator to say exactly that, for months.

quiz.question: What does the narrator conclude about apologies at the end?
options: They get easier the longer you wait
They rarely get easier with time; they usually get heavier
They are unnecessary between old friends
Only the other person should apologize first
quiz.explanation: He concludes apologies rarely become easier by waiting; they usually just become heavier and harder to say.
